lines.trans: Thank you, I am not hungry.
I do not eat after six.
Katya, please forgive me.
I really do have tons of work.
Alright, I am waiting for you.
Come to the suite quickly.
Kiss me.
What are you doing, huh?
The Chef will kill me.
Calm down, I am talking to Siri.
You lie right here for now.
Lie there for now and work up an appetite.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'пасибо'). Common neuter noun meaning 'thank you' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('hungry').

examples.trans: Thank you, Chef, I am very hungry!

examples.text: Наши гости в зале очень голодные.
examples.trans: Our guests in the hall are very hungry.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'after', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Он за мной после концерта ухаживал.
examples.trans: He courted me after a concert once.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian cardinal or ordinal numeral meaning 'six', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to eat', paired with 'съесть'.

examples.text: Я вчера ел маринованные грибы. Может, один гриб был плохой.
examples.trans: Yesterday I ate pickled mushrooms. Maybe one mushroom was bad.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'Katya' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть кать.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always Katya.
The chef immediately noticed where the Katya was.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'come on, well', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'стить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'forgive', paired with 'прощать'.
High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, near, with', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Ой, кажется, у вас сломан нос!
examples.trans: Oh, it looks like your nose is broken!

examples.text: Завтра у меня важное собеседование на работу.
examples.trans: Tomorrow I have an important job interview.

examples.text: Значит, у нас с тобой много общего.
examples.trans: So you and I have a lot in common.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'really', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Правда, Нин, всё нормально. Скажи что-нибудь, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: Honestly, Nina, everything's fine. Say something, please.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'job, work' in everyday Russian.
Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: There are plenty of people there.

examples.text: А почему мой шашлык никто не ест? Мяса полно!
examples.trans: And why is nobody eating my shashlik? There's plenty of meat!

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: All right, here you go. There, look.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'am waiting for', paired with 'подождать'.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to come', paired with 'прийти'.

examples.trans: If you change your mind, come back. The job is waiting.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'корее').

examples.trans: Let's go quickly to the studio!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'number' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Don't laugh. Read me the number.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'целовать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'kiss', paired with 'целовать'.
High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.en: to do, to get up to (something outrageous)
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'you are doing', paired with 'сотворить'.

examples.text: Он сам не понимает, что творит.
examples.trans: He doesn't know what he is doing himself.

examples.text: Самсоновы, вы что творите? Хватит, я прошу вас!
examples.trans: Samsonovs, what are you doing? Stop it, I beg you!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'but, after all', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'бить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'will kill', paired with 'убивать'.

examples.trans: Do you want to kill me?

examples.text: Ты смотришь на меня так, как будто убить хочешь.
examples.trans: You look at me as if you want to kill me.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'покойно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Его не будет часа два. Вы спокойно всё сделаете.
examples.trans: He'll be gone for about two hours. You'll do everything calmly.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'Siri' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: На кухне отеля всегда есть сири.
examples.trans: In the hotel kitchen there is always Siri.
The chef immediately noticed where the Siri was.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'speak', paired with 'сказать'.
High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'for now', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The owner is busy in the kitchen for now.

meanings.en: to lie, to be lying down, to rest
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'lie there', paired with 'полежать'.

examples.text: Такие люди должны лежать в особенном месте!
examples.trans: Such people should lie in a special place!
The book is lying on the table.
But I'll be lying next to Grishka for eternity.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.
Common masculine noun meaning 'appetite' in everyday Russian.
Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'гуливать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'work up'.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и нагуливать вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and work up on time.

examples.text: На нашей кухне все умеют нагуливать.
examples.trans: In our kitchen everyone knows how to work up.
